::: {.why}
Path-dependent logic is the one case where a loop is the right algorithm, and it is exactly where pure Python is slowest, which is a narrow but real gap worth closing.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Compile one path-dependent function with numba and report the speedup against the pure Python and the vectorised versions.
- Say what numba cannot compile and how you find out before deploying it.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Compile your loop in no-python mode and measure it against the pure Python version and against any vectorised approximation. Report all three times and confirm the outputs match. Path-dependent code often shows two orders of magnitude, which is the largest single gain available in this phase.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [20 min]{.task-min} Find the boundaries: numba silently falls back to object mode unless you forbid it, which produces code that is slower and looks compiled. Force strict mode, then deliberately write something it cannot compile and observe the error rather than the silent fallback.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Rerun the benchmark harness and record the new baseline, so the phase's cumulative improvement is a number rather than an impression.
:::
:::
